strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: fast data assimilation for high-dimensional dynamics under extremely sparse spatial and temporal observations.
The proposed integration of latent dynamics, history-aware LSTM observation encoding, and score-based filtering is intuitive and clearly presented.
Experiments cover two nontrivial PDE systems and report state reconstruction, parameter estimation, observation-noise sensitivity, and runtime.
The reported results are promising: LD-EnSF substantially improves RMSE over EnSF and Latent-EnSF while greatly reducing online computation.
weaknesses: The latent likelihood central to the filter is not adequately defined or justified. Equation 18 assumes an identity observation map and additive latent noise after a nonlinear, history-dependent LSTM transformation, but the paper does not explain how the latent-noise distribution or covariance is estimated. Consequently, the score term required by EnSF is underspecified.

The LSTM alone already predicts latent states and parameters with very low reported test error, yet there is no LSTM-only baseline. It is therefore unclear whether score-based assimilation contributes meaningfully beyond direct supervised sequence estimation.

The evaluation lacks essential ablations, including current-only versus historical observations, filtering versus direct encoding, noisy versus noiseless encoder training, reconstruction retraining, latent dimension, ensemble size, and observation sparsity or frequency.

Comparisons are limited to EnSF and Latent-EnSF. Strong standard and learned alternatives such as EnKF variants, latent EnKF methods, recurrent state estimators, or other latent data-assimilation approaches discussed in the related-work section are omitted.

Results are based on two synthetic, in-distribution settings without repeated trials, error bars, statistical tests, out-of-distribution parameters or initial conditions, alternative sensor layouts, or uncertainty-calibration metrics. This is insufficient for broad robustness and Bayesian posterior-quality claims.

The speed comparison excludes offline training and appears to compare a learned low-dimensional surrogate against full numerical simulation. It does not establish comparable accuracy or account clearly for hardware and implementation effects, so the claimed 2,000x to 200,000x acceleration is not an end-to-end controlled comparison.

Important implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing, including the latent likelihood, diffusion discretization and step count, score damping and noise settings, normalization at inference, and training or evaluation variability. The ensemble size also differs between the described experiments and the timing table.

The methodological novelty is primarily a combination of existing LDNets, LSTMs, and EnSF. Given the unresolved likelihood formulation and incomplete empirical isolation of each component, the evidence does not yet support acceptance at a top-tier AI venue.

The combination of latent dynamics, history-aware observation encoding, and latent-space filtering is coherent and clearly presented. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/e22a9a9af67343c9ac46b2a55b2dd1d0/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The experiments cover two nonlinear PDE systems and report results under spatially and temporally sparse observations with several noise levels. Comparisons include the most directly related EnSF and Latent-EnSF methods.
The learned latent spaces are very small, and the reported online speedups are substantial. The paper also provides useful architecture and optimization details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic formulation is insufficiently specified. Equation (18) treats the nonlinear, history-dependent LSTM output as the true augmented latent state plus additive noise, but the paper neither derives nor validates this model. It does not explain how the induced latent-noise distribution or covariance is estimated, despite the EnSF update requiring the likelihood score. LSTM approximation error will generally be state-dependent, temporally correlated, and non-Gaussian, so this omission affects both soundness and reproducibility.

The benchmarks largely reduce data assimilation to low-dimensional static parameter identification. Shallow-water trajectories are determined by two Gaussian-bump coordinates, while Kolmogorov trajectories use a fixed initial condition and vary only a scalar Reynolds number. There is no process noise, unparameterized model error, or arbitrary uncertain high-dimensional initial state. An LSTM can therefore infer the static parameter and associated deterministic trajectory from observation history; this does not convincingly demonstrate general high-dimensional state filtering.

Critical ablations are absent. The paper does not compare against directly decoding the LSTM estimate, using only the current observation, replacing EnSF with a latent EnKF or simpler update, omitting parameter prediction, or omitting reconstruction-network retraining. Consequently, the results do not establish that score filtering is necessary or identify which component produces the gain.

The baseline evaluation is too narrow for a top-tier conference. There are no comparisons with EnKF or latent EnKF, variational assimilation, particle-based methods, or other learned latent filters. Moreover, the authors acknowledge that their Latent-EnSF baseline uses much less training data than the original work and appears undertrained, weakening the fairness of the main accuracy comparison.

Although the method is presented as Bayesian assimilation, evaluation is almost entirely state RMSE. There is no assessment of posterior calibration, ensemble spread, coverage, parameter uncertainty, or multimodal recovery. Results lack repeated-run variability or confidence intervals and appear to rely on a very small number of illustrated trajectories.

Robustness is tested only by changing observation-noise magnitude under the same fixed sensor pattern and in-distribution trajectory family. There are no sweeps over spatial or temporal sparsity, sensor placement, ensemble size, latent dimension, longer forecasting horizons, or out-of-distribution parameters and initial conditions.

The efficiency comparison omits offline training and hyperparameter-search costs, mixes CPU dynamics timings with GPU reconstruction timings, and uses ensembles of 20 in the accuracy experiments but 100 in the timing table. These choices make the claimed end-to-end real-time advantage difficult to assess.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the exact definition of percentage noise, the latent likelihood used by EnSF, diffusion discretization and hyperparameters, aggregation of reported errors, random seeds, training cost, and code availability.

The methodological novelty is incremental: it primarily combines an existing LDNet architecture, a standard LSTM, and EnSF. The stated LDNet modifications—changing initialization and retraining the reconstruction network—are modest, and no theoretical analysis compensates for the limited methodological novelty. Overall, the idea is promising but the evidence does not support the paper's broad claims of robust, accurate high-dimensional Bayesian data assimilation.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: fast high-dimensional data assimilation under extremely sparse and noisy observations.

The integration of latent dynamics, history-aware LSTM observation encoding, and ensemble score filtering is coherent and potentially useful; joint estimation of states and uncertain parameters is a valuable feature.
Experiments cover two nontrivial PDE systems, including turbulent Kolmogorov flow, with only 0.44% spatial observations and multiple noise levels.
Reported results are promising: LD-EnSF substantially improves RMSE over EnSF and Latent-EnSF while reducing the assimilation dimension to roughly 10–12 and producing very large online speedups.
The paper is generally clear, includes informative visualizations, and provides useful architecture and training details.
weaknesses: The latent likelihood central to EnSF is insufficiently specified. The paper assumes the deterministic LSTM output satisfies an identity observation model with additive latent noise, but does not clearly define or estimate the distribution/covariance of that noise or explain how its likelihood score is computed. This limits technical validation and reproducibility.

The LSTM alone already predicts latent states and parameters with very low test error, yet there is no LSTM-only baseline. Consequently, the experiments do not establish how much the score-filtering stage contributes beyond a supervised history-to-state estimator.

Key ablations are missing, including observation history versus current observations, direct latent prediction versus filtering, the second reconstruction-training stage, latent dimension, ensemble size, observation density, and temporal sparsity.

Comparisons are restricted mainly to EnSF variants. Strong standard and latent-space alternatives such as EnKF/LETKF, latent EnKF, particle filtering, or other learned assimilation methods are absent, weakening the claim of broad competitiveness.

The reported speedups largely compare a learned surrogate against full numerical simulation, omit offline training and amortization costs, and mix CPU and GPU timings. They therefore do not isolate the computational benefit of the proposed filtering method itself.

Evaluation uses only two synthetic systems within the training parameter distributions and time horizons. There is no out-of-distribution, longer-horizon, or real-observation experiment, despite claims concerning robustness and real-time applicability.

Results lack repeated-run statistics, uncertainty calibration, posterior-quality metrics, and error bars. Important implementation details such as diffusion discretization, likelihood parameters, random seeds, and complete simulator settings are also missing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: accelerating high-dimensional data assimilation under sparse observations by performing both forecasting and filtering in a compact latent space.

The proposed integration of improved latent dynamics networks, a history-aware observation encoder, and ensemble score filtering is intuitively motivated and produces substantial online speedups over full-space simulation-based methods.

The empirical study covers three nontrivial dynamical systems and includes useful ablations and sensitivity analyses for latent dimension, ensemble size, observation density, surrogate accuracy, architectural choices, noise distributions, and modest distribution shifts.

The learned surrogate is compact and accurate in the tested in-distribution settings, and the experiments consistently show lower state-estimation RMSE than EnSF, Latent-EnSF, and the reported classical baselines.

The manuscript is generally well organized and provides extensive architectural and training details. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/b9595df186ed452591c9799446ca798d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The filtering formulation is not Bayesianly justified when the LSTM observation at time t encodes the complete history y_1:t. Consecutive latent observations reuse nearly all earlier measurements and therefore have strongly correlated errors, but Equations 9–10 repeatedly treat them as ordinary new likelihood factors. This can double-count evidence and undermines the claimed posterior and uncertainty interpretation.

The supervised LSTM is trained to directly recover both the latent state and the unknown physical parameters from simulated observations and already achieves extremely low test error. Consequently, much of the result may come from an amortized inverse model rather than EnSF. The LSTM-only ablation is helpful but insufficient: the paper does not compare EnSF with simpler filters or uncertainty mechanisms using exactly the same encoder and latent dynamics.

Uncertainty evaluation is inadequate for a method framed as Bayesian filtering. Most reported uncertainty bands appear to summarize variation across test trajectories rather than posterior calibration, and there are no coverage, reliability, log-likelihood, or multivariate calibration results. The observation model further replaces correlated, biased, state-dependent encoder errors with a scalar latent noise level. The finding that one ensemble member performs similarly to larger ensembles reinforces concern that posterior sampling contributes little.

Baseline coverage and tuning are not convincing enough for the strong superiority claim. Comparisons focus on the precursor methods and LETKF; 4DEnVar appears only for one task, several relevant learned latent-filtering or neural data-assimilation methods are discussed but not evaluated, and details such as localization, inflation, reverse-SDE discretization, and baseline hyperparameter selection are missing. LETKF divergence is also attributed to a CFL issue without sufficient diagnosis.

The evaluation is entirely simulator-generated and predominantly in distribution, with only 200 trajectories per problem. The atmospheric experiment is an idealized forced shallow-water system rather than realistic operational weather assimilation. The reported OOD experiment shows rapid degradation and does not evaluate the full assimilation pipeline under meaningful shifts, model error, changing sensors, or real observations.

The claim of handling arbitrary or irregular observations is overstated. The method supports a fixed irregular sensor layout after training a new LSTM for that layout; it does not accept sensor coordinates and requires retraining when observation locations change. This substantially limits practical applicability.

The speed comparison largely measures replacement of an expensive numerical solver by an offline-trained surrogate, mixes CPU and GPU components, and reconstructs the full LD-EnSF state only at the final step. Data-generation and training costs are not consistently incorporated into headline speedups, while the break-even discussion is ambiguous about cycles, trajectories, and ensemble size.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript's code link is blank, and important EnSF numerical settings, experimental seeds, complete noise definitions, and baseline configurations are not specified. Overall, the empirical promise is notable, but the probabilistic formulation and evaluation do not sufficiently support the central filtering and uncertainty claims for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly organized and presents an intuitive end-to-end framework combining latent dynamics, history-aware observation encoding, and score-based filtering. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/f6768847504646e6a8398dd4df0bbe5f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The experiments cover three physically distinct systems and include useful studies of observation noise, irregular sensors, latent dimension, ensemble size, observation density, surrogate accuracy, and architectural components.
Operating entirely in a small latent space produces substantial online speedups, and the reported surrogate and reconstruction accuracy is generally strong.
The comparison with VAE-based latent dynamics illustrates a practical advantage of learning smooth, explicitly evolved latent trajectories.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly establish a genuinely high-dimensional filtering problem. Each benchmark is generated from only one or two uncertain parameters, often with a fixed initial condition, so the admissible trajectories occupy a very low-dimensional supervised family. An LSTM can largely identify those parameters from observation history and reconstruct the deterministic trajectory; this is much easier than state estimation under high-dimensional initial-condition uncertainty, process noise, or model error.

The proposed latent observation model is not justified as a valid Bayesian likelihood. The LSTM maps the entire history y_1:t to a point estimate of the latent state and parameters, after which the method assumes an identity observation operator with additive noise. Because successive encodings contain overlapping past observations, treating each as a new observation can repeatedly count the same evidence. The paper provides neither a sufficiency argument nor a derivation showing that the resulting recursion targets p(kappa_t | y_1:t).

The empirical latent-noise model is particularly weak: it replaces the encoder error with a scalar standard deviation shared across latent dimensions, discarding bias, correlations, heteroskedasticity, temporal dependence, and state dependence. Robustness to scaling this scalar does not validate the posterior or uncertainty estimates.

The novelty is limited. The main construction combines an existing EnSF, an existing LDNet, and a standard supervised LSTM. The LDNet changes—shifted initialization, decoder fine-tuning, ResNet blocks, and Fourier features—are mostly modest or established techniques. The experiments do not clearly separate gains from the score filter from gains due simply to supervised inverse regression and surrogate forecasting; indeed, the reported ensemble-size study says that one member performs similarly.

Baseline coverage and tuning are inadequate for the claims. Despite discussing numerous learned latent-space, Koopman, particle-filter, and neural data-assimilation methods, the main comparisons are largely EnSF, Latent-EnSF, and LETKF. LETKF localization, inflation, ensemble size, and tuning are insufficiently documented, and its atmospheric failure is attributed to numerical instability without a careful diagnosis. 4DEnVar is included for only one benchmark.

The runtime comparison primarily demonstrates that a learned low-dimensional surrogate is faster than repeatedly solving a full PDE. It mixes CPU, 64-CPU, and GPU measurements, excludes most reconstruction costs for LD-EnSF, and does not give a rigorous end-to-end comparison including data generation, hyperparameter search, all training costs, and equivalent output requirements. The appendix's break-even calculation is also difficult to reconcile with the reported units and trajectory-level timings.

The experiments use only 200 simulated trajectories with in-distribution train/validation/test splits. The limited OOD study shows rapidly degrading error, and a new observation encoder must be trained for every sensor configuration. There is no real observational dataset, misspecified physical model, changing sensor layout, missing-data pattern, or high-dimensional stochastic uncertainty to support the real-time deployment claims.

Uncertainty evaluation is insufficient. Error bands and one CRPS plot do not demonstrate calibrated posterior samples, coverage, or reliable extreme-event uncertainty; the observation that ensemble size has little effect further calls into question whether the score-based ensemble machinery contributes meaningful posterior inference.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the stated code link is blank, several important EnSF implementation and tuning details are absent, and many headline results are reported only graphically without numerical tables or variability across seeds. Overall, the extensive experiments are promising, but the central Bayesian interpretation and broad claims are not adequately supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: LD-EnSF is a coherent and practically motivated framework that moves both forecasting and filtering into a compact latent space, enabling joint state and parameter estimation without online full-space simulation.
The history-aware LSTM encoder is well motivated for extremely sparse observations, and the ability to handle irregular sensor locations is useful, although sensor layouts require retraining.

The evaluation is unusually broad: three high-dimensional physical systems, structured and unstructured observations, multiple noise levels and noise distributions, parameter estimation, out-of-distribution tests, runtime measurements, and extensive sensitivity analyses.

Results consistently favor LD-EnSF over EnSF, Latent-EnSF, VAE-dyn, and the reported classical baselines. The approximately 5% error on the atmospheric benchmark with roughly 0.1% spatial coverage is particularly encouraging.

Ablations substantiate several design choices, including the modified LDNet, Fourier/ResNet reconstruction, fine-tuning, temporal observation encoder, latent dimension, and the contribution of filtering beyond direct LSTM reconstruction.
The paper is generally clear and supplies substantial architectural, training, data-generation, and offline-cost information in its appendices.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is primarily an effective integration of existing ingredients—LDNet, LSTM encoding, and EnSF—plus incremental LDNet modifications. The paper provides limited theoretical insight into when the resulting latent Bayesian update is valid.

Comparisons do not cover several closely related learned or reduced-space assimilation approaches discussed in the paper, such as latent EnKF/particle filters, Koopman-based filtering, Deep Bayesian Filtering, 4DVarNet-style methods, or recent score-based alternatives. Moreover, 4DEnVar is evaluated only for tsunami modeling, and the atmospheric LETKF result is omitted after divergence without enough tuning or diagnostic detail.

All experiments use synthetic trajectories generated from the same model family used for training, with uncertainty confined to a few low-dimensional parameters. This does not test substantial model error, real observations, spatially varying uncertain fields, or major distribution shifts; the limited OOD experiment already shows steady degradation.

The LSTM defines a deterministic, history-dependent pseudo-observation, yet its residual is modeled with an identity observation map and a scalar Gaussian uncertainty estimated using reference latent states. Temporal correlations, state dependence, and non-Gaussian latent errors are not modeled, so the claimed Bayesian posterior interpretation is only approximate.

Uncertainty evaluation is limited. Uncertainty bands and one CRPS sensitivity experiment do not establish posterior calibration, coverage, or reliability, and the statement that a single ensemble member effectively yields a MAP estimate is insufficiently justified.

The headline speedups compare an amortized learned surrogate against expensive numerical solvers and largely emphasize online cost. Although offline training cost is reported, heterogeneous CPU/GPU execution and limited end-to-end break-even analysis make the orders-of-magnitude claim less directly comparable across methods.

Reproducibility is weakened by the apparently blank code link and by missing implementation and tuning details for several baselines, including localization, inflation, and the cause of LETKF instability. Overall, the empirical evidence supports a marginal accept, but these issues keep the work below a confident score of 8.
